question: What is shadowing, and how is it different from repeating?
coach: Shadowing means speaking along with a clip a split second behind the speaker, while you're still hearing it. Repeating is different: you listen, pause, then say it back. Shadowing is the harder, more live version, because you can't stop to think.
keywords: what is shadowing definition repeating repeat difference shadowing définition répéter différence qu'est-ce que sombra definición repetir diferencia qué es
answer: Shadowing means repeating speech out loud while you are still hearing it, a fraction of a second behind the speaker, usually without reading a script. Listen-and-repeat is different: you hear a chunk, there is a pause, then you say it. Researchers treat shadowing as the more demanding "live" version because you cannot stop to think about meaning. The word is used loosely, though: in one systematic review, 8 of 44 studies that said "shadowing" actually used delayed repetition of single words.

sources.cite: Hamada, Y. (2019). Shadowing: What is it? How to use it. Where will it go? RELC Journal, 50(3), 386-393.
sources.finding: Origin in interpreter training; Lambert's (1992) definition 'a paced, auditory tracking task which involves the immediate vocalization of auditorily presented stimuli'; contrast with repetition (offline, chunk by chunk).

sources.cite: Whitworth, B., & Rose, H. (2025). A systematic review of research on the use of shadowing for second language pronunciation teaching. Research Synthesis in Applied Linguistics, 1(2), 239-269. (journal and pages confirmed via Crossref)
sources.read: full text (introduction, methods, results; the final discussion section not read)
sources.finding: Defines shadowing as simultaneous speaking and listening with a short lag, versus classical listen-and-repeat; found 8 of the 44 included studies did not use the technique as defined.

caveats: Hamada's classification of 16 shadowing variants (Hamada & Suzuki 2022) is secondhand.
not_say: That a particular lag is best (not researched yet).

question: How good is the evidence that shadowing works?
coach: Yes, it's worth doing. Most studies find it helps, and the clearest benefit is for listening. It also seems to help how easy you are to understand, how fluent you sound and your rhythm. Don't expect it to fix every individual sound, though, and nobody can promise how much it will change your accent.
keywords: help helps evidence research studies proof proven work works scientific science really effective preuve preuves recherche études efficace fonctionne scientifique evidencia investigación estudios funciona eficaz científico
answer: There is real research and most of it is positive, but it is thin. The best evidence is for listening. For pronunciation, a 2025 systematic review of 44 studies tentatively concluded shadowing can help how easy you are to understand, plus fluency and rhythm/intonation, while results for individual sounds were inconclusive. The studies are mostly short, mostly with learners of English (many in Japan or Taiwan), and usually tested with controlled tasks like reading aloud, so nobody knows how much it helps you in particular or how much practice is ideal.

sources.cite: Whitworth & Rose (2025), see A1.
sources.design: systematic review, 44 studies found, 34 analysed (8 excluded for not being shadowing, 2 dissertations merged with their later papers)
sources.finding: Of the 26 studies that directly tested pronunciation improvement, 11 used overall measures; 2 of those used a composite speaking test the authors call inconclusive for pronunciation, and of the other 9 (comprehensibility, intelligibility, accentedness) 7 were positive and 7 used only controlled tasks. The authors conclude 'tentatively' that shadowing can help. 8 measured fluency: all positive. 11 measured prosody: mostly positive, several with weak reporting. 4 measured segmentals: mixed or methodologically weak, so inconclusive. 20 studies used only controlled tasks (such as reading aloud). L2: 27 English, 5 Japanese, 1 French (none Spanish). Perceptions generally positive (see F1).

sources.cite: Hamada (2019), see A1.
sources.finding: Most studies ran about a month; the optimal amount of practice has not been identified; delayed post-tests are lacking; most work is in Japan; speaking studies often have weak design, questionable analysis, and rely on self-report.

caveats: Whitworth & Rose graded studies themselves; I did not check individual studies.
Hamada ran several of the studies he reviews.
not_say: That shadowing beats other methods (direct comparisons are few).
That a set number of weeks changes an accent.

question: Does shadowing improve pronunciation and accent?
coach: It can help you become easier to understand and sound more fluent, especially if you're already fairly advanced. The clearest gains are in clarity and flow rather than in how accented you sound, and it's less certain for fixing single sounds. So use it for rhythm and flow, and don't expect it to wipe out an accent on its own.
keywords: pronunciation accent improve improvement sounds speaking better help helps prononciation accent améliorer progresser pronunciación acento mejorar
answer: It may help how easy you are to understand and how fluent you sound, especially for advanced learners. The one carefully rated study I read found gains in comprehensibility and fluency but not in how accented the speech sounded. Evidence for fixing individual sounds is inconclusive.

sources.cite: Foote, J. A., & McDonough, K. (2017). Using shadowing with mobile technology to improve L2 pronunciation. Journal of Second Language Pronunciation, 3(1), 34-56.
sources.design: 16 participants (described by Hamada as high-proficiency), 8 weeks, at least 4 times a week, at least 10 minutes, iPod recordings of short dialogues (sitcoms per Hamada); pre/mid/post tests rated by 22 English speakers
sources.finding: Significant improvement on all measures except accentedness; participants were positive about the activity.

sources.cite: Whitworth & Rose (2025), see A1.
sources.finding: Overall pronunciation measures: of 9 usable studies, 7 positive (see A8); segmentals inconclusive; Hori (2008) found no improvement.

sources.cite: Hamada (2019), see A1.
sources.finding: Reports Hamada (2016b, a Routledge book that I have not opened): 29 intermediate Japanese university students, about a month at about 20 minutes twice a week, shadowing compared with a repetition group, 6 native-speaker raters, little improvement in comprehensibility or accentedness in either group (secondhand).

caveats: Small samples, short interventions, usually read-aloud or shadowing-recording tests.
Foote & McDonough had no comparison group in the abstract as I read it.
not_say: That shadowing will remove an accent.

question: Does shadowing improve listening?
coach: Listening is where shadowing helps most. After a few weeks of regular shadowing, learners in several classes understood spoken English better, and the gain was biggest for people whose listening was weaker. Whether the gain lasts after you stop hasn't been tested, so keep it up.
keywords: listening comprehension understand hearing listen écoute compréhension orale comprendre escucha comprensión auditiva entender
answer: Listening is the best-supported benefit. Several classroom studies, mostly in Japan and Taiwan, report better listening scores after a few weeks of shadowing, and one study found better recognition of individual sounds. The gains in that study were mainly for learners with lower listening levels.

sources.cite: Hamada, Y. (2016). Shadowing: Who benefits and how? Uncovering a booming EFL teaching technique for listening comprehension. Language Teaching Research, 20(1), 35-52.
sources.design: 43 Japanese university students, 9 lessons, 22-question listening test and 20-item dictation test, before and after
sources.finding: Phoneme perception improved in both the low- and intermediate-level groups; listening-question scores improved only in the low-level group.

sources.cite: Hamada (2019), see A1.
sources.finding: Summarises classroom studies (Kato 2009, Tamai 1997, Lin 2009; all secondhand) with listening gains; suggests shadowing trains bottom-up listening (hearing words).

caveats: No control group in Hamada's abstract design as described; short interventions.
Mostly Japanese EFL learners.
not_say: That the gains last after you stop (delayed tests are lacking).

question: Who benefits most?
coach: Shadowing works at most levels, but it suits you better the closer the clip is to what you can already follow. If your listening is still developing, you'll likely gain a lot. If you want to copy a fast, natural speaker's sounds closely, it helps to be fairly comfortable first. Choose slower or easier clips if you keep losing the thread.
keywords: beginner advanced level who benefits suitable proficiency débutant avancé niveau principiante avanzado nivel
answer: For listening, lower-level learners seem to gain most (one study, plus reports of others). For pronunciation, the study with clear gains used advanced learners, and one author argues you need a fairly high level to copy a fast, natural speaker accurately. That is the author's reading of two different studies, not a test of the question.

sources.cite: Hamada (2016), see A3.
sources.finding: Listening gains only in the low-level group.

sources.cite: Foote & McDonough (2017), see A2.
sources.finding: Gains in comprehensibility/fluency with high-proficiency speakers.

sources.cite: Hamada (2019), see A1.
sources.finding: Recommends beginners start with shadowing for listening, then move to shadowing for speaking; this recommendation is the author's inference.

caveats: No study I read compared levels for pronunciation in the same experiment.

question: How often and how long should I shadow?
coach: A few short sessions a week beat one long one. In the studies that worked, people shadowed three or four times a week, at least 10 minutes each, for a month or two. That's a good rule of thumb rather than a proven number, so choose a routine you'll actually stick to.
keywords: how often how long daily every day minutes weekly frequency practice schedule spacing session length combien fréquence jours minutes quotidien chaque jour cuántas frecuencia días minutos diario todos los días
answer: Nobody has tested how often or how long to shadow. The studies that worked used a few short sessions a week for a month or two (for example, 4 times a week for at least 10 minutes over 8 weeks). Memory research on other material says spreading practice over days beats cramming it, so several short sessions with gaps is a sensible bet, but that is borrowed evidence, not a shadowing result.

sources.cite: Foote & McDonough (2017), see A2.
sources.finding: At least 4 sessions a week, at least 10 minutes, 8 weeks.

sources.cite: Hamada (2014) The Language Teacher 38(1), 3-10 (see D1) and Hamada (2019).
sources.finding: Hamada's own study: twice a week for a month. Hamada (2019): optimal amount of practice not identified; other schedules (e.g. 15 min a week for 5 months; 90 min over 5 days; 50 min three times a week for 5 weeks) are secondhand.

sources.cite: Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354-380.
sources.design: meta-analysis, 839 assessments, 317 experiments, 184 articles
sources.finding: Spacing helps retention; the best gap grows with how long you need to remember.

sources.cite: Cepeda, N. J., Vul, E., Rohrer, D., Wixted, J. T., & Pashler, H. (2008). Spacing effects in learning: A temporal ridgeline of optimal retention. Psychological Science, 19(11), 1095-1102.
sources.design: more than 1,350 people taught facts, gaps up to 3.5 months, test up to a year later
sources.finding: Optimal gap rose with test delay; as a share of the delay it fell from about 20-40% (1 week) to about 5-10% (1 year); gaps that were too short cost more than gaps that were too long.

sources.cite: Lee, J., Jang, J., & Plonsky, L. (2015). The effectiveness of second language pronunciation instruction: A meta-analysis. Applied Linguistics, 36(3), 345-366.
sources.finding: Across pronunciation instruction in general (86 reports), longer interventions had larger effects. Not specific to shadowing.

caveats: Spacing studies used facts, not speech practice; applying them is my inference.
No shadowing study compared schedules.
not_say: That any number of sessions, minutes or days is optimal.

question: Should I use a transcript, or understand the clip first?
coach: If you can't follow a clip yet, read what it says first, then shadow it. That order is a sensible way to start. Once you know the clip well, try it without the text so you're listening to the sounds, not reading. There's no proven rule here, so do whatever helps you stay with the speaker.
keywords: transcript subtitles script text read understand first captions transcription sous-titres texte lire transcripción subtítulos leer
answer: Classic shadowing is defined as scriptless, although the lessons in that study included reading along with the text. In the one study that tested order (two different classes, no control group), the class that learned the passage first and shadowed afterwards gained 0.84 of 13 points on a listening test, a statistically significant gain; the class that shadowed first gained 0.53, which was not significant. Nobody tested whether the two gains differ from each other. Nobody I found compared "with transcript" and "without" for pronunciation, so there is no evidence-based rule. If you can't follow a clip yet, knowing what it says first has only that one small study behind it.

sources.cite: Hamada, Y. (2014). The effectiveness of pre- and post-shadowing in improving listening comprehension skills. The Language Teacher, 38(1), 3-10.
sources.design: 56 Japanese first-year university students (intermediate), two classes (32 and 24), 8 lessons over a month, 13-item TOEIC-type listening test; no control group
sources.finding: Group that shadowed after learning vocabulary and content: gain of 0.84 points out of 13, significant (p<.05, r=.41). Group that shadowed before: gain of 0.53, not significant (p>.05).

sources.cite: Hamada (2019), see A1.
sources.finding: Defines shadowing as scriptless; describes 'text-presented shadowing' as a variation that changes what learners attend to; reports the pre/post result consistently with the 2014 paper.

caveats: RESOLVED: the abstract of the 2014 paper swaps the group labels. The full text (steps, table, results) and Hamada 2019 agree that the group that improved shadowed AFTER learning the content.

Listening scores, not pronunciation. The two groups were different intact classes (engineering vs international communication) and the difference between their gains was not tested; small effect, one month, no control group, one teacher (the author lists these as limitations). The lessons included shadowing while reading the text and a text check.
Claims that scripts make shadowing more effective (Kuramoto et al. 2007; Kuramoto & Matsumura 2001) are secondhand and not opened. Euno must not repeat them as findings.
The French subtitle study (J1) suggests learners lean on subtitles when repeating; whether that helps or hurts accent is not tested.
not_say: That a transcript helps or hurts pronunciation or accent.
app_note: Euno compares you with the speaker's audio, not with a transcript.

question: Does recording myself and checking it help?
coach: Record yourself and listen back afterwards. While you shadow, all your attention is on the speaker, so you can't judge your own voice in the moment. Checking your recording afterwards is a good habit, and the small studies on it point the same way, though it isn't proven.
keywords: record recording myself self listen back playback monitor enregistrer enregistrement m'écouter grabar grabación escucharme
answer: Two small Japanese studies, described in a review, compared self-monitoring (recording yourself and checking it) with pair-checking or other checking methods. In one, the self-monitoring group reproduced more of the clip; in the other, only lower-level listeners in the self-monitoring group improved on listening questions. I haven't opened those studies, so treat this as a lead, not a finding. The idea behind it: while you shadow, all your attention is on the audio, so you can't judge yourself in the moment.

sources.cite: Hamada (2019), see A1.
sources.finding: Reports Nakayama & Suzuki (2012; 35 students in three groups: self-monitoring with a recorder and script check, pair-monitoring with the script, and a control who checked by recalling their performance; the self-monitoring group did better on reproduction rate) and Hamada (2015; 61 sophomores, pair-shadowing vs self-monitoring, 30 minutes twice a week for a month; only low-proficiency listeners in the self-monitoring group improved on listening questions). Both secondhand.

sources.cite: Lee, Jang & Plonsky (2015), see B1.
sources.finding: Across pronunciation instruction, treatments that gave feedback had larger effects (not specific to self-recording).

caveats: Primary studies not opened; one is in Japanese.

question: Is a native accent the right goal?
coach: Being understood and sounding like a particular speaker are two different goals. A strong accent doesn't automatically make you hard to understand, and clarity matters most for most people. If sounding close to your chosen speaker is what you want, that's a perfectly good goal. Just know that it's a personal choice, not something you need.
keywords: native accent goal intelligible intelligibility comprehensible foreign lose accent natif objectif intelligible compréhensible acento nativo meta inteligible
answer: Researchers separate three things: how accented you sound, how easy you are to understand, and how many words listeners actually catch. A classic study found that a strong accent does not necessarily make speech hard to understand. Many researchers now treat clarity as the main goal, but sounding close to a model speaker is a legitimate personal goal if that's what you want (that last point is our judgement, not a research finding).

sources.cite: Munro, M. J., & Derwing, T. M. (1995). Foreign accent, comprehensibility, and intelligibility in the speech of second language learners. Language Learning, 45(1), 73-97.
sources.design: 18 English-speaking listeners rated and transcribed speech from 10 Mandarin speakers and 2 English speakers
sources.finding: Accent strength correlated with perceived comprehensibility and intelligibility, but a strong accent did not necessarily reduce either.

sources.cite: Whitworth & Rose (2025), see A1.
sources.finding: Describes the 'intelligibility principle' vs 'nativeness principle' (Levis 2005, 2020; secondhand) and reports that among the studies with pronunciation measures (31 in its tables; which set exactly is not fully clear), only 2 were based on intelligibility measures versus 12 on nativeness (4 both, 13 unclear).

caveats: One small study of Mandarin speakers learning English; the wider claim rests on later work I haven't opened.

question: Does pronunciation teaching work at all?
coach: Yes, practising pronunciation on purpose works. On average people improve clearly, and more with longer programmes and with feedback on what to fix. Results vary a lot from person to person, so expect steady progress rather than a quick fix.
keywords: teaching pronunciation instruction lessons teacher taught learn enseignement enseigner cours professeur enseñanza clases profesor
answer: Yes, on average. A meta-analysis of 86 reports found a large improvement from pronunciation instruction, bigger for longer programmes and ones that include feedback. The authors warn that published results probably overstate the true effect, and a separate review notes many studies tested only read-aloud speech.

sources.cite: Lee, Jang & Plonsky (2015), see B1.
sources.finding: d = 0.89 (before/after) and 0.80 (vs control); larger for longer interventions, feedback, and more controlled outcome measures; funnel plot suggests publication bias; no studies of children in the typical critical-period range.

sources.cite: Thomson, R. I., & Derwing, T. M. (2015). The effectiveness of L2 pronunciation instruction: A narrative review. Applied Linguistics, 36(3), 326-344.
sources.finding: 75 studies; mixed results despite many reports of improvement; most aimed at native-like pronunciation; read-aloud tests common, spontaneous speech rare; some lacked control groups.

caveats: Not about shadowing specifically.
The funnel-plot and critical-period statements come from an excerpt of the article body; the independent check could not open the full text to confirm them.

question: Does ear training help me pronounce a sound?
coach: Listening closely to a hard sound, with lots of different speakers, helps a little with saying it. The gains are small though, so don't count on listening alone. Listen carefully, then say it out loud and compare.
keywords: ear training perception hear difference minimal pairs perceive production entraînement auditif perception paires minimales entrenamiento auditivo percepción pares mínimos
answer: Training your ear on a hard sound with many speakers gives small gains in how you say it, with weaker gains on new words and over time. The authors of the newer review say the evidence that hearing training transfers to speaking is not strong. These studies did not test whether you must hear a sound before you can say it.

sources.cite: Sakai, M., & Moorman, C. (2018). Can perception training improve the production of second language phonemes? A meta-analytic review of 25 years of perception training research. Applied Psycholinguistics, 39(1), 187-224.
sources.finding: Perception training: medium gains in perception (d=0.92), small gains in production (d=0.54); the link between perception and production gains was small-to-medium and not statistically significant.

sources.cite: Uchihara, T., Karas, M., & Thomson, R. I. (2024). Does perceptual high variability phonetic training improve L2 speech production? A meta-analysis of perception-production connection. Applied Psycholinguistics, 45(4), 591-623.
sources.design: 31 studies
sources.finding: Small-to-medium production gains (10.5% on trained items, 4.5% on untrained); no strong support for long-term retention or generalisation; the perception-production link was negligible at the participant level and moderate only at the level of whole studies.

caveats: Perception training studies, not shadowing.

question: Does automatic feedback on pronunciation help? How accurate is it?
coach: Feedback from software can help, mostly when it tells you exactly which sound to fix. Treat a flag as a prompt to listen again, not a verdict. Software can mark clear speech as wrong, and Euno's sound differences haven't been checked against what real listeners hear.
keywords: automatic feedback software app score grade accurate accuracy asr ai computer retour automatique logiciel score précis précision note ia retroalimentación automática puntuación precisión
answer: On average, software feedback on pronunciation helps, mostly for individual sounds and when it tells you specifically what to fix. The reviews also say the evidence is of limited quality and one review notes, secondhand and not independently confirmed, that this kind of software can mark understandable speech as wrong, so a flag is a prompt to listen again, not a verdict.

sources.cite: Ngo, T. T.-N., Chen, H. H.-J., & Lai, K. K.-W. (2023). The effectiveness of automatic speech recognition in ESL/EFL pronunciation: A meta-analysis. ReCALL.
sources.design: 15 studies, 38 effect sizes
sources.finding: g = 0.69 overall; explicit corrective feedback 'largely effective' and indirect feedback 'moderately effective' (g = 0.86 vs 0.50, values taken from an excerpt of the article body and not confirmed by the independent check); large effect for individual sounds, small for stress/rhythm/intonation; short treatments showed no difference from non-ASR conditions.

sources.cite: Mahdi, H. S., & Al Khateeb, A. A. (2019). The effectiveness of computer-assisted pronunciation training: A meta-analysis. Review of Education.
sources.design: 20 studies, 1,014 participants
sources.finding: d = 0.68 for computer-based versus traditional teaching (not specifically feedback), but the authors call the studies small and low quality, so the evidence is 'indicative and not conclusive'.

sources.cite: Amrate, M., & Tsai, P. (2024). Computer-assisted pronunciation training: A systematic review. ReCALL.
sources.finding: 30 studies, mostly adult learners of English and controlled drills; In its body text (not confirmed by the independent check), citing Henrichsen (2021), it says systems still struggle to evaluate L2 speech accurately and can mark comprehensible speech as wrong; treat as secondhand.

caveats: None of these reviews tests shadowing or Euno's method.
App-specific: Euno's sound flags (speaker clip vs your take) have not been checked against listener judgments. NOT verified.

question: Is shadowing boring? Will I stick with it?
coach: Most learners find shadowing interesting and useful. Some find it repetitive or frustrating, especially when the audio is too fast. If it starts feeling like a chore, switch to a slower or more interesting clip rather than pushing through.
keywords: boring bored motivation stick quit enjoy tedious repetitive ennuyeux ennui motivation abandonner aburrido motivación abandonar
answer: Most learners in the studies found shadowing interesting and useful. A minority found it repetitive, time-consuming or frustrating when the audio was too fast, and some got discouraged after failing. I found no study on streaks or reminders for shadowing.

sources.cite: Whitworth & Rose (2025), see A1.
sources.design: 16 perception studies, mostly questionnaires, many teacher-collected
sources.finding: Interest and enjoyment reported across ages; recurring complaints: fast audio, repetitiveness, boredom, procrastination, demotivation after failure; one survey of 36 advanced learners of Japanese found somewhat more complaints among lower-level students.

sources.cite: Hamada (2014), see D1.
sources.finding: Notes shadowing's high cognitive load and repetitive nature as possible downsides; unfamiliar content raised anxiety in some learners (reported from another source).

caveats: Perception data are self-reports.
not_say: That streaks, reminders or rewards raise adherence (not researched).

question: Does shadowing work for French or Spanish?
coach: Shadowing should work for French and Spanish too, but nearly all the research is on English, so it's a sensible bet rather than a proven one. Euno's sound-by-sound comparison only works for English at the moment.
keywords: french spanish language other languages français espagnol langues francés español idiomas lenguas
answer: Almost all the research is on English. In the 2025 systematic review, 27 of 34 analysed studies were about English, 5 about Japanese and 1 about French; none about Spanish. A small French study with 19 high-school students found better pronunciation after a term of repeat-after-the-video practice, but it wasn't strict shadowing and had no comparison group. So for French and Spanish Euno should say shadowing is plausible but untested.

sources.cite: Whitworth & Rose (2025), see A1.
sources.finding: L2 counts as above (27 + 5 + 1 + 1 unreported = 34).

sources.cite: Martinsen, R., Montgomery, C., & Willardson, V. (2017). The effectiveness of video-based shadowing and tracking pronunciation exercises for foreign language learners. Foreign Language Annals.
sources.read: abstract; plus the earlier BYU thesis version (Willardson 2014) excerpts
sources.design: 19 fourth-year high school French students, 3 times a week over a term, subtitled videos; pre/post read-aloud and free-response tests
sources.finding: Significant improvement on both tasks, most on read-aloud; in the thesis, students mostly read subtitles while repeating, which may explain the read-aloud gain; in the thesis 'shadowing' meant repeating after a pause when needed.

caveats: I assume the one French study in the review is Willardson/Martinsen; not confirmed.
Two student theses on shadowing for French and Spanish learners turned up (a Colombian monograph on French and a US Spanish club study with 5 online sessions); not reviewed, qualitative, so not used.
app_note: Euno's sound comparison is English-only; for French and Spanish clips it does not check sounds.

question: Which French sounds are hardest for English speakers?
coach: The sounds English speakers most often struggle with in French are the front rounded vowels, like the u in tu versus the ou in tout, and peur versus port. Nasal vowels and liaison are often hard as well. Listen to those pairs carefully and shadow short phrases that contain them. Euno's sound comparison is English-only for now.
keywords: french sounds hard difficult vowels sons français difficiles voyelles sonidos francés difíciles vocales
answer: The best-documented trouble spot is telling the front rounded vowels (like the u in "tu" versus "tout", and "peur" versus "port") apart (the study tested hearing and word recognition, not speaking); even advanced English-speaking learners categorise these differently from French speakers. Nasal vowels and liaison are often listed as hard too, but I have not yet found solid studies to cite for them.

sources.cite: Darcy, I., Dekydtspotter, L., Sprouse, R. A., Glover, J., Kaden, C., McGuire, M., & Scott, J. H. G. (2012). Direct mapping of acoustics to phonology: On the lexical encoding of front rounded vowels in L1 English-L2 French acquisition. Second Language Research.
sources.finding: US English-speaking learners find /y/-/u/ and /oe/-/open o/ contrasts hard; intermediate and advanced learners categorised them differently from native speakers.

caveats: Perception/categorisation study; says little about how to train it.

question: Which Spanish sounds are hardest for English speakers?
coach: Common trouble spots for English speakers in Spanish are the soft b, d and g between vowels (lado, haba), the rolled r versus the single tap (carro and caro), and p, t and k without a puff of air. The soft b, d and g take time, so expect gradual progress. Euno's sound comparison is English-only for now.
keywords: spanish sounds hard difficult vowels trill sons espagnol difficiles voyelles sonidos español difíciles vocales vibrante
answer: Studies point to the soft b/d/g between vowels (as in "lado", "haba"), the rolled r versus the tap ("carro" vs "caro"), and unaspirated p/t/k. The soft b/d/g is hard for learners: in one year-long study of 26 learners, looking at the soft b only, the group average did not change, although some individuals improved.

sources.cite: Nagle, C. L. (2017). Individual developmental trajectories in the L2 acquisition of Spanish spirantization. Journal of Second Language Pronunciation, 3(2).
sources.design: 26 English-speaking learners, 5 recordings over a year
sources.finding: Group trajectory flat; many individuals changed, positively or negatively.

sources.cite: Face, T. L., & Menke, M. R. Acquisition of the Spanish voiced spirants by second language learners. Hispanic Linguistics Symposium proceedings.
sources.finding: Earlier studies (e.g. Zampini 1994, secondhand) found learners generally failed to spirantise in most expected cases in early semesters (exact percentage not verified). Face & Menke (2009, Selected Proceedings of the 11th Hispanic Linguistics Symposium, pp. 39-52): 53 learners in three groups; Ph.D.-level learners spirantised in over 80% of expected contexts.

sources.cite: Herd, W., & Sereno, J. (2008). Tracking non-native acquisition of the Spanish tap-trill distinction. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 124(4 Suppl.), 2594.
sources.read: abstract (conference abstract, 8 learners vs 8 native speakers)
sources.finding: Perception (cross-modal priming), not production: learners process intervocalic taps differently from native speakers. A fuller paper exists (Herd, Sereno & Jongman 2015, Studies in Hispanic and Lusophone Linguistics, DOI 10.1515/shll-2015-0005); not yet read.

sources.cite: Reeder, J. T. (1998). English speakers' acquisition of voiceless stops and trills in L2 Spanish. Texas Papers in Foreign Language Education.
sources.finding: 40 college learners at four levels; trill is acquired differently from voiceless stops.

caveats: Small studies; vowel reduction and stress are not covered yet.

question: Is French/Spanish "syllable-timed", and does it matter?
coach: Copy the speaker's real timing instead of trusting the textbook idea that Spanish and French have an even beat. Measurements don't show a clean split between languages. Shadow closely and let the speaker's rhythm guide you.
keywords: syllable-timed stress-timed rhythm syllable timed french spanish rythme syllabique accentuel ritmo silábico acentual
answer: Textbooks call Spanish and French "syllable-timed" and English "stress-timed", but measurements don't back a clean split. One study of six languages found the rhythm numbers were inconsistent, affected by how speech was recorded, and not clearly different even between English and Spanish. So "copy the speaker's real timing" is safer advice than "Spanish has an even beat".

sources.cite: Arvaniti, A. (2012). The usefulness of metrics in the quantification of speech rhythm. Journal of Phonetics, 40(3), 351-373.
sources.design: 8 speakers each of English, German, Greek, Italian, Korean, Spanish; three kinds of speech
sources.finding: Classifications were inconsistent across measures; differences were often non-significant even between English and Spanish; scores depended heavily on elicitation method and syllable complexity.

caveats: French was not in that study.
This is a measurement study, not a learning study.

question: How far behind the speaker should I be?
coach: Stay a short, comfortable beat behind the speaker, roughly a quarter to half a second, so you can still hear them while you speak. No one has found a best exact delay, so adjust until it feels steady.
keywords: lag delay behind how far behind latency seconds speaker close distant décalage retard derrière combien de retard desfase retraso detrás cuánto retraso
answer: I found no study that tested which delay works best for learning. Psychology experiments, as described in a Japanese study, divide shadowers into "close" (about a quarter of a second behind) and "distant" (about half a second or more); that split is secondhand here. In a study of 81 Japanese high school students there was almost no link between how long learners waited and how many errors they made, and the author proposed more than a second as the definition of a long delay. A short, comfortable lag is how shadowing is described, but a best number is not established.

sources.cite: Marslen-Wilson, W. (1973). Linguistic structure and speech shadowing at very short latencies. Nature, 244, 522-523.
sources.finding: Shadowers can start repeating a sentence before hearing all of it; response latency per word can be measured.

sources.cite: Miyake, S. (2009). Cognitive processes in phrase shadowing: Focusing on articulation rate and shadowing latency. JACET Journal, 48, 15-28.
sources.finding: Describes Marslen-Wilson (1985) as splitting people into 'close' shadowers (mean delay about 250 ms) and 'distant' shadowers (about 500 ms or more), both processing syntax and meaning. The 250/500 ms figures are secondhand (Marslen-Wilson via Miyake). The study itself: 30 Japanese undergraduates, phrase shadowing, hypothesis that better listeners shadow with longer latency; results not read.

sources.cite: Oki, T. (2010). The role of latency for word recognition in shadowing. Annual Review of English Language Education in Japan (ARELE), 21 (J-STAGE KJ00007108609).
sources.design: 81 Japanese high school students; a deviant word was placed in the passage (not pseudo-words)
sources.finding: Almost no association between latency group and error rates. 'Over one second' is the author's proposed definition of long latency, not a finding. The delay 'may be as long as the shadower can afford'.

sources.cite: Whitworth & Rose (2025), see batch 1 (A1).
sources.finding: In practice shadowing involves a short lag between stimulus and repetition.

caveats: Lab studies of native speakers, plus small learner studies; none compared lags for improvement.
Marslen-Wilson 1973 was seen only as a snippet and the 1985 split is secondhand via Miyake; Miyake's results were not read.
not_say: That 250 ms, or any specific lag, is ideal for learning.
app_note: Euno measures your lag, but there is no research-backed target value for it.

question: What speed should I shadow at? Should I slow the audio?
coach: Start slower, then speed up over a few weeks as it gets comfortable. Slowed audio helps you pick out the sounds, and pushing the speed too early mostly causes frustration. Go back to natural speed as soon as you can keep up, since that's the speed you'll meet in real life.
keywords: speed slow slower faster fast rate slow down audio words per minute vitesse lent plus lent rapide ralentir velocidad lento más lento rápido ralentizar
answer: Starting slower is supported, though by little shadowing-specific evidence. A study that trained listening with slowed recordings found the slow group improved most at hearing individual sounds and words. In a Japanese-as-a-foreign-language shadowing study, the author suggests beginning slowly and speeding up over weeks, but listening improved in both the shadowing and the control group there, so it does not show speed-ups matter. Experiments with bilinguals show shadowing accuracy falling steadily once speech goes beyond about 125 words per minute. Pushing speed too early can cause frustration, which is a recurring complaint in learner surveys.

sources.cite: McBride, K. (2011). The effect of rate of speech and distributed practice on the development of listening comprehension. Computer Assisted Language Learning, 24(2).
sources.finding: Four groups trained with fast, slow, chosen-speed, or pausable audio; the slow group did best, apparently because bottom-up processing improved; others developed strategies that transferred less well; learners did better when training was spread over several days. Listening training, not shadowing.

sources.cite: Sumiyoshi, H. (2019). The effect of shadowing: exploring the speed variety of model audio and sound recognition ability in the Japanese as a foreign language context. e-FLT (Electronic Journal of Foreign Language Teaching), 16(1). DOI 10.56040/hdsm1611 (confirmed via Crossref).
sources.design: 29 university students of Japanese in Australia (experimental vs control), 8 weeks, model speed raised from 315 to 440 morae per minute
sources.finding: Listening improved significantly in both groups, with no group or interaction effect. Dictation differed: the shadowing group improved at slow and fast speed, the control group only at slow speed. Two existing courses, not randomised. The author reads the weekly data as suggesting benefit from fast (400+ morae/min) rather than slow audio, and recommends starting slow to avoid anxiety. A suggestion of 90-95% shadowing accuracy as the right challenge and the 'fast speed benefits' reading were not located again in an independent check, so treat them as unverified.

sources.cite: van Paridon, J., Roelofs, A., & Meyer, A. S. (2019). A lexical bottleneck in shadowing and translating of narratives. Language, Cognition and Neuroscience.
sources.design: 20 Dutch-English bilinguals, speech at 100-200 words per minute
sources.finding: Shadowing was at ceiling at 100 and 125 words per minute, then declined roughly in a straight line as speech got faster.

sources.cite: Whitworth & Rose (2025) and Hamada (2019), see batch 1.
sources.finding: Fast audio is a recurring learner complaint.

caveats: Different languages and tasks; the numbers do not transfer to a particular clip.
No study found a best speed for pronunciation learning.
Sumiyoshi's 90-95% and fast-speed statements are unverified (an independent reader could not find them).
not_say: That slowed audio gives the same pronunciation gain as natural speed.

question: How many times should I repeat the same clip?
coach: A handful of repeats of the same clip is enough. After about four or five, you copy it about as well as you're going to, so more rounds add little. Move to a new clip and come back to the old one on another day.
keywords: repetitions repeat times how many same clip again répétitions répéter fois combien repeticiones repetir veces cuántas
answer: In one experiment, after four or five repeats of the same passage, learners' accuracy at copying it levelled off close to its ceiling, so more repeats of that one passage added little to accuracy. A newer study found learners who did more repeats scored higher on listening and phrase-memory tests. Neither tested pronunciation, so a best number of repeats for accent is not established.

sources.cite: Shiki, O., Mori, Y., Kadota, S., & Yoshida, S. (2010). Exploring differences between shadowing and repeating practices. Annual Review of English Language Education in Japan, 21, 81-90.
sources.design: 48 university students, shadowing and repeating, six trials each
sources.finding: Four or five trials were enough to bring the reproduction rate near its ceiling; shadowing reproduced more content words than repeating.

sources.cite: Hashizaki, R., Sekiyama, H., Xing, Y., & Wakita, K. (2025). Exploring the optimal number of repetitions for shadowing. JALT Journal, 47(1).
sources.design: 30 Japanese university students, 11 weekly 90-minute sessions
sources.finding: More repetitions went with higher post-test scores in listening and multiword expressions; bottom-up processing and repetition speed improved regardless of the number of repetitions.

sources.cite: Muraoka, Y. (2017). Shadowing and fluency. Keisen University repository.
sources.design: 8 Japanese college students, 11 weeks
sources.finding: No significant improvement in fluency measures.

sources.cite: Boers, F. (2014). A reappraisal of the 4/3/2 activity. RELC Journal.
sources.finding: Repeating the same talk three times improved fluency (adjacent: speaking, not shadowing); much of the gain came from reusing the same word strings.

caveats: Shiki et al. measured how much of the clip learners reproduced, not whether their pronunciation got better.
Hashizaki's repetition counts include practice outside class, so more repeats may reflect more motivated learners.
not_say: That 4-5 repeats is the right number for pronunciation.

question: Can I improve by shadowing alone, with no teacher?
coach: Yes, you can practise alone at home. In one study, beginners shadowing every day for six weeks improved their listening, but didn't clearly improve their own pronunciation. So pair it with recording yourself and checking, or with feedback, if accent is the goal.
keywords: alone self-study teacher own myself independent seul tout seul sans professeur solo sin profesor autoaprendizaje
answer: One conference study had 35 Japanese beginner learners of English (CEFR A1-A2) shadow short passages at home every day for six weeks with no teacher and no control group. A score of their hearing improved, but across the 42 days I could see no clear gain in their own pronunciation, although within a single session their shadowing got closer to the model. It is a single study and the perception score is an automatic score of their own shadowing, so treat it as a hint.

sources.cite: Kunihara et al. (2022). Gradual improvements observed in learners' perception and production of L2 sounds through continuing shadowing practices on a daily basis. Interspeech 2022.
sources.design: 42-day programme, four new ~30 s passages per day, each shadowed three times plus once with the script; recorded at home; speech slowed to 0.8 then 0.9 in the first four weeks; 20 participants attended every day
sources.finding: 35 participants (A1-A2), no control group. Perception score (an automatic score of the learners' own shadowing) improved; within-session production got closer to the model, but across the 42 days there was no clear gain in production. I say 'no clear gain', not 'no gain'.

sources.cite: Lee, Jang & Plonsky (2015), see batch 1 (B1).
sources.finding: Instruction that gives feedback has larger effects.

caveats: A conference paper; no control group; Japanese beginner learners of English.
Pronunciation was measured by a method I did not read in full.
not_say: That self-study cannot work, only that this study saw no clear production gain.

question: Does sleep help? Should I practise before bed?
coach: Practising in the evening may help it stick, because sleep helps memory settle. That's a mild hint from lab studies on hearing new sounds, not a rule, so practise whenever you'll really do it.
keywords: sleep bed night tired consolidation memory evening morning sommeil dormir nuit soir matin sueño dormir noche tarde mañana
answer: In lab studies of learning a foreign speech sound (not shadowing), people trained in the evening and tested the next day did better than people trained in the morning, which suggests sleep helps the memory settle. These were small experiments on hearing a sound difference, so they do not show that shadowing before bed helps.

sources.cite: Earle, F. S., & Myers, E. B. (2015). Sleep and native language interference affect non-native speech sound learning. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance.
sources.finding: Participants trained on a non-native contrast at night improved in discrimination 24 hours later; those trained in the morning showed no such improvement; hearing similar native-language sounds during the day may interfere.

sources.cite: Earle, F. S., & Myers, E. B. (2013). The effect of sleep on learned sensitivity to a non-native phonetic contrast. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America.
sources.design: 54 monolingual English speakers, Hindi dental-retroflex contrast
sources.finding: Discrimination improved after the overnight interval in the night group, declined slightly in the morning group.

sources.cite: Earle, F. S., & Myers, E. B. (2014). Overnight consolidation promotes generalization across talkers in the identification of nonnative speech sounds. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America.
sources.finding: Overnight consolidation promoted generalisation across talkers in identification, not necessarily in discrimination.

sources.cite: Earle, F. S., Landi, N., & Myers, E. B. (2016). Sleep duration predicts behavioral and neural differences in adult speech sound learning. Neuroscience Letters, 636, 77-82. PMC5152565.
sources.finding: Light-sleep duration predicted gains in identification and total sleep predicted gains in discrimination; small sample (about 18 participants, inferred from reported statistics).

caveats: Perceptual training on one foreign contrast, small samples. No shadowing or production data.
not_say: That practising right before bed improves shadowing results.

question: I'm nervous or embarrassed. Does anxiety matter?
coach: Feeling nervous about speaking is common, and it tends to go along with slower progress. Starting with slower or familiar clips can take some of the pressure off.
keywords: anxiety nervous embarrassed shy afraid stress self-conscious anxiété stress nerveux gêné timide honte ansiedad nervioso vergüenza tímido
answer: Language anxiety is real and measurable. A large analysis of 97 reports found a moderate negative link between anxiety and language achievement, though that is a correlation, not proof that anxiety causes poorer results. For shadowing, the evidence is thinner: researchers and learners say it is demanding to repeat unfamiliar speech, and starting with familiar or slower material is suggested to reduce stress.

sources.cite: Teimouri, Y., Goetze, J., & Plonsky, L. (2019). Second language anxiety and achievement: A meta-analysis. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 41(2), 363-387.
sources.design: 97 reports, 105 samples, N = 19,933, 23 countries
sources.finding: Mean r = -0.36 between L2 anxiety and achievement, varying by measure, educational level, target language and anxiety type.

sources.cite: Horwitz, E. K., Horwitz, M. B., & Cope, J. (1986). Foreign language classroom anxiety. Modern Language Journal.
sources.finding: Defines foreign language anxiety as related to communication apprehension, test anxiety and fear of negative evaluation; speaking and listening are the centre of the problem for anxious students.

sources.cite: Hamada (2014), see batch 1 (D1).
sources.finding: Argues, as his interpretation, that knowing the passage first can ease the stress of shadowing; notes that shadowing has a high cognitive load.

sources.cite: Sumiyoshi (2019), see C9.
sources.finding: Recommends starting slow to avoid anxiety (author's suggestion).

caveats: Teimouri's figure covers language achievement in general, not pronunciation or shadowing.
Two student theses on recording yourself and anxiety turned up; they are unpublished and I did not use them.
not_say: That practising alone with recordings reduces anxiety (not established).

question: Why are some people better at copying accents?
coach: People differ in how easily they copy an accent. A good ear for music and quick, flexible mouth movements help, and so does liking the speaker. None of that says how much you can improve with practice, so don't read a slow start as a ceiling.
keywords: talent gift ear music imitate imitation accents personality ability talent don oreille musique imitation aptitude talento don oído música imitación aptitud
answer: People differ a lot in how well they can imitate an accent, and studies link it to a good ear for music, quick mouth movements, and personality traits such as openness; attitudes towards the speaker also play a part. These are studies of how well people copy, not of how much training improves them, so they say nothing about how much you can gain by practising.

sources.cite: Myers, Olson, & Scapetis-Tycer (2024) [first names not captured]. Individual differences in accent imitation. Open Mind, 8, 1084-1106. PMC11370968.
sources.finding: Imitation of three accents was predicted by musical perception, articulatory agility and openness, and was affected by attitudes towards the imitated talker.

sources.cite: Lewandowski, N., & Jilka, M. (2019). Phonetic convergence, language talent, personality and attention. Frontiers in Communication.
sources.design: 20 German speakers talking with 2 English speakers
sources.finding: Speakers rated as phonetically talented converged more toward their partners.

sources.cite: Hutchinson, A. E. (2022). Individual variability and the effect of personality on non-native speech shadowing. JASA Express Letters, 2(6), 065203.
sources.design: 74 English speakers shadowed French words containing /y/ and /u/
sources.finding: Higher extraversion and neuroticism scores went with closer matches on one acoustic measure (F1) but not another (F2). Whitworth & Rose list this study among the 8 that did not use shadowing as they define it, so it is not evidence about shadowing; the F1/F2 detail was not independently verified.

caveats: Small, short lab studies; mixed measures; none measured long-term improvement.
not_say: That your 'talent' limits what you can reach.

question: Is it true that shadowing works because of mirror neurons?
coach: You don't need to worry about mirror neurons. You sometimes hear that they explain why shadowing works, but that idea isn't proven, and the practice works as advice either way. Just keep shadowing and listening back to yourself.
keywords: mirror neurons neuroscience brain why neurones miroirs cerveau neuronas espejo cerebro
answer: I found no study showing that mirror neurons explain why shadowing helps. Some shadowing papers mention mirror neurons as a possible reason, and at least one calls the idea "still controversial". A critical review argues that the mirror-neuron explanation of how we understand actions has never been properly tested and faces strong evidence against it in humans. The practical advice about shadowing doesn't depend on it.

sources.cite: Kunihara et al. (2022), see E4.
sources.finding: Introduction mentions mirror neurons as a rationale and describes the idea as 'still controversial' (author's own caveat).

sources.cite: Hickok, G. (2009). Eight problems for the mirror neuron theory of action understanding in monkeys and humans. Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience, 21(7), 1229-1243.
sources.finding: No direct monkey evidence tests the theory that mirror neurons underlie action understanding, and human evidence argues against it.

caveats: Hickok's paper is about action understanding, not language learning; it challenges the strong claim, it does not show that mirror neurons play no role in imitation.
not_say: That mirror neurons do or do not exist in humans, or that shadowing doesn't work.

question: I've stopped improving. Is that normal?
coach: Yes, it's normal. Most people progress fast at the start, then slower, and a lot of people hit flat patches. A plateau doesn't mean you should stop. Change clips, speaker or speed, or go back to your notes on what's still off, and keep going.
keywords: plateau stuck stopped improving progress slow plateau bloqué stagner progresser meseta estancado estancamiento progresar
answer: Yes, it's a common pattern. Studies that followed adults learning English by living in it found fast progress in the first months or years, then slower progress, with large differences between people. Some people kept improving for years, though most levelled off. None of this measured shadowing, so I cannot say how a shadowing plateau looks.

sources.cite: Munro, M. J., & Derwing, T. M. (2008). Segmental acquisition in adult ESL learners: A longitudinal study of vowel production. Language Learning, 58(3).
sources.design: 44 recent arrivals in Canada, recordings every 2 months
sources.finding: Vowel intelligibility improved about 10 points in a year without focused instruction, mostly in the first half of the year, then levelled off.

sources.cite: Derwing, T. M., & Munro, M. J. (2013). The development of L2 oral language skills in two L1 groups: A 7-year study. Language Learning.
sources.finding: Mandarin-speaking group showed no change on comprehensibility, fluency or accent over 7 years; Slavic-language group improved in comprehensibility and fluency; accent improved only in the first 2 years.

sources.cite: Thomson, R. I., Derwing, T. M., & Munro, M. J. (2024). How long can naturalistic L2 pronunciation learning continue in adults? A 10-year study. Language Awareness, 33(2), 201-223.
sources.finding: Some speakers kept improving from year 7 to 10 but most plateaued or regressed.

caveats: Immigrants learning English by living in it, not deliberate practice; small samples (18 speakers at year 10).
not_say: That a plateau means you should stop, or that it can't be broken.

question: Can shadowing strain my voice?
coach: If your voice feels tired, hoarse or sore, rest it and keep sessions short. There's no research on voice strain from shadowing, so this is common sense, not a study result.
keywords: voice strain hoarse sore throat tired vocal voix fatigue enrouée gorge voz cansancio ronca garganta
answer: I found no study of voice strain from shadowing. The nearest evidence is one small study in which people said their voice tired faster when speaking a foreign language, but measurements mostly suggested this may come from mental effort rather than extra vocal loading, though some measures hinted at more loading. If your voice feels hoarse or sore, that's a reason to rest, not something research can tell you more about here.

sources.cite: Järvinen, K., & Laukkanen, A.-M. (2015). Vocal loading in speaking a foreign language. Folia Phoniatrica et Logopaedica (Karger), 67(1) (journal confirmed via Crossref short title).
sources.design: 20 Finnish and 23 English native speakers recorded in both languages
sources.finding: Speakers reported faster voice fatigue in the foreign language; measured vocal doses were lower, and the authors suggest the feeling may reflect mental stress. Some measures (the level difference between L1 and L0, normalised doses) hinted at more loading.

caveats: Does not study shadowing, imitation of a different pitch, or long practice sessions. Health advice here is common sense, not research.
not_say: That shadowing is safe or unsafe for your voice.

question: Does seeing the spelling help or hurt my pronunciation?
coach: Reading along can help you catch a sound, and it can also pull you toward the wrong pronunciation, like saying letters that are silent. French spelling is especially tricky for this, since many letters are silent. A good approach is to read first if you need to, then shadow without the text to focus on the sounds.
keywords: spelling orthography written letters reading silent orthographe lettres écrit lire ortografía letras escrito leer
answer: Both. A review of this research finds that written words can help learners hear and say a sound, and can also push them toward wrong pronunciations, like pronouncing silent letters. Which happens depends on how the spelling matches your own language's spelling-sound habits. This is the closest evidence for the transcript question, but none of it tested shadowing.

sources.cite: Hayes-Harb, R., & Barrios, S. (2021). The influence of orthography in second language phonological acquisition. Language Teaching.
sources.finding: Written input can affect L2 phonological awareness, perception, and pronunciation; effects depend on whether the writing system represents a sound contrast systematically, whether letters are familiar, whether letter-sound mappings match the L1, and whether the contrast can be perceived.

sources.cite: Bassetti, B., & Atkinson, N. (2015). Effects of orthographic forms on pronunciation in experienced instructed second language learners. Applied Psycholinguistics, 36(1), 67-91.
sources.design: four studies with Italian-speaking learners of English, about 10 years of experience
sources.finding: Spellings affected the pronunciation of known words, more in reading aloud than in repeating.

sources.cite: Bassetti, B. (2008). Orthographic input and second language phonology. In Piske & Young-Scholten (Eds.), Input Matters in SLA.
sources.finding: Reports that Chinese beginner learners of French pronounced a French uvular fricative in clusters more accurately when they saw the word written (Steele 2005, secondhand), and that English and Turkish speakers repeated Irish and Spanish words more accurately when they saw them written (Erdener & Burnham 2005, secondhand). The same secondhand report notes harm in one case: Turkish speakers with Irish spelling.

caveats: French spelling-to-sound is irregular and Spanish is regular; no study here compares them for shadowing.
Bassetti 2008 findings about Steele and Erdener are secondhand.
not_say: That shadowing with subtitles or a transcript improves or harms your accent.

question: French: nasal vowels and liaison
coach: Two things English speakers often find tricky in French are the nasal vowels (the ones in blanc and bon) and liaison, where a silent final consonant links to the next word, as in petit ami. Listen to short phrases with those, shadow them slowly, and compare. Euno's sound comparison is English-only for now.
keywords: french nasal vowels liaison blanc bon linking voyelles nasales liaison vocales nasales enlace
answer: English speakers learning French do find some contrasts harder than others. In one comparison, English speakers were less accurate than Spanish speakers at telling apart two nasal vowels (the ones in "blanc" and "bon") and made them sound more alike. For liaison (linking a normally silent final consonant, as in "petit ami"), two studies of English-speaking learners point the same way: one (Howard 2005) finds obligatory liaison produced near-categorically but optional liaison used less than by native speakers; another (Tennant 2015) finds liaison closer to native rates in spontaneous speech than in reading aloud. These are two separate findings, not one result.

sources.cite: Chanethom, V., & Mather, P.-A. (2019). Perception and production of French nasal vowel contrasts by English- and Spanish-speaking L2 learners. [journal via DOAJ, not captured]
sources.design: 10 English-speaking and 10 Spanish-speaking learners, reading and discrimination tasks
sources.finding: English speakers were less accurate at the /ɑ̃/ vs /ɔ̃/ contrast and produced smaller acoustic differences between them; Spanish speakers showed no particular difficulty.

sources.cite: Tennant, J. (2015). Canadian anglophone learners' realization of French liaison. [journal: see DOI]
sources.design: 12 Ontario anglophone speakers, reading, interview, discussion
sources.finding: Liaison rate approached native speakers in spontaneous speech but was lower in reading aloud; non-linking in 7.2% of liaisons, falling with more years of study. Variable liaison did not vary by task.

sources.cite: Howard, M. (2005). L'acquisition de la liaison en français langue seconde.
sources.finding: Advanced anglophone learners produce obligatory liaison near-categorically but not in every context; variable liaison is used less than by the native speaker.

sources.cite: Wauquier, S., & Shoemaker, E. M. (2013). Convergence and divergence in the acquisition of French liaison by native and non-native speakers. Language, Interaction and Acquisition, 4(2).
sources.finding: Overview of production and psycholinguistic findings on L1 and L2 liaison.

caveats: Journals for Chanethom & Mather, Tennant and Howard are unconfirmed.
Small groups; reading words, not connected speech. Nasal vowel work by Charlton (a conference poster, 11 advanced learners) not used as a citation.
A PhD thesis (de Moras 2011) reports a group that practised repetition improved most in liaison; not used because it's an unreviewed thesis I read only in part.
not_say: That these are the only French difficulties, or that nasal vowels are harder than front rounded vowels (one training study found nasal vowels were learned faster; it is a student thesis).

question: French and Spanish stress and intonation
coach: In French, the stress falls at the end of a phrase, and the voice tends to rise there. In Spanish, stress usually lands where English speakers expect, except in words stressed on the last syllable. Listen for where the speaker puts the weight, and copy the tune of a whole phrase, not just word by word.
keywords: stress intonation prosody pitch french spanish rise placement accent tonique intonation prosodie acento tónico entonación prosodia
answer: The rhythm of French and Spanish differs from English at the phrase and word levels. In one production study, English-speaking learners of Spanish placed stress like native speakers except in words stressed on the last syllable, while learners of French were less accurate and tended to stress too early or in several places, because French marks prominence at the end of phrases. Another study found English speakers struggled to group French words into the right phrases and to produce the phrase-final rise. These are small studies, so use them as hints about what to listen for.

sources.cite: Colantoni, L., Marasco, O., Steele, J., & Sunara, S. Phonological and phonetic aspects of the L2 acquisition of French and Spanish stress. Proceedings of LARP 6.
sources.finding: 5 L2 French and 5 L2 Spanish speakers, descriptive statistics only. Learners of French were less accurate than learners of Spanish at stress placement; French learners tended to stress earlier in the phrase and produced multiple primary stresses; Spanish learners were target-like except for final-stressed words; vowels in unstressed syllables were centralised by French learners but not Spanish learners.

sources.cite: Lee, S. (2014). The realization of French rising intonation by speakers of American English. Speech Prosody 2014.
sources.design: 8 American college students starting a study-abroad term in southern France
sources.finding: Struggled with grouping words into accentual phrases and with the phonetic realisation of phrase-final rises; pitch range was smaller than French speakers'.

caveats: Conference proceedings; small samples (Colantoni et al. 5+5, descriptive only). Lee is Scott Lee of the University of Georgia; Colantoni et al. first names not captured.
Spanish intonation questions are not covered.
not_say: That these patterns hold for all learners or all varieties.

question: Which Spanish or French accent should I copy?
coach: Pick the speaker you want to understand and sound like, and stay with them for a while. The more different voices you hear, the better you'll understand them. Some accents are harder at first, but it passes after a few weeks. There's no proven best variety to copy.
keywords: regional variety dialect which accent copy spanish french argentine mexican spain quebec europe variété régionale dialecte quel accent copier québec variedad regional dialecto qué acento copiar argentino mexicano
answer: Research on learners of Spanish found that familiarity with a regional variety went with better understanding of it, and understanding was more accurate with several kinds of exposure (a correlation, not a proven cause). Some varieties are harder at first (for example, Argentine "y/ll" sounds caused recognition problems in a four-week immersion study, which went away after a month). There is no evidence on which variety is best to copy for pronunciation, so pick the speaker you want to understand and sound like.

sources.cite: Schoonmaker-Gates, E. (2018). Dialect comprehension and identification in L2 Spanish: Familiarity and type of exposure. Studies in Hispanic and Lusophone Linguistics.
sources.design: 60 L1 English learners, transcription and dialect-identification tasks across six regions
sources.finding: Familiarity predicted (correlation, not cause) identification at all levels and comprehension for more advanced learners; comprehension was more accurate with multiple types of exposure, and with exposure from native instructors, study abroad and media.

sources.cite: Schmidt, L. B. (2023). Effects of dialect exposure on the processing of Argentine regional phones by English-speaking L2 learners of Spanish. ICPhS 2023, paper 305.
sources.design: 22 learners, no control group; 4-week study abroad in Buenos Aires, lexical decision tasks in week 1 and week 4
sources.finding: Initially less accurate on words with the Argentine palatal sound; this effect disappeared by week four, while slower processing of words with aspirated /s/ persisted.

caveats: Perception and comprehension only; no study on what to copy in production. French varieties not covered (one reference to Quebec vs European French vowel learning seen but not opened).
A broader review of L2 Spanish dialect perception (University of Arizona journal) was used only to find these sources.
not_say: Which Spanish or French variety produces better pronunciation gains.
